sections.heading: Thanking you for the gift of faith
sections.text: My God, thank you for giving me faith—not as something I produced in myself, but as a gift of your grace. By faith you have opened my eyes to know you as my Father, to trust you as the God who keeps his promises, and to recognize your love at work inside me. Through faith I am joined to Christ, and in him I can say, with humble confidence, that I belong to you and that you have given yourself to me.
theological_themes: Faith is a gracious gift from God, not a human achievement.
Through faith, the believer knows God as Father and rests in his covenant promises.
Faith unites the believer to Christ and gives humble assurance of belonging to God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that salvation by grace through faith is not self-generated but God's gift, which supports the prayer's gratitude for faith as something received from God.
This passage grounds the believer's confidence in approaching God as Father and sharing in the inheritance of Christ, which fits the prayer's language of belonging to God through faith.
Paul describes life by faith as life in union with Christ, showing that faith is not bare belief but participation in Christ's life and love.

sections.heading: Holding on to you as my Lord
sections.text: Let my trust reach upward to you like an anchor fastened where I cannot see. Keep me from drifting into self-rule or fear. I entrust myself to you again: be my Lord, my safety, my future, and my rest.
theological_themes: Faith looks beyond visible circumstances and holds fast to God.
Trust in God includes yielding to his lordship.
The believer's security is anchored in God's faithfulness, not in personal strength.

scripture_references.connection: The image of an anchor reaching into God's presence supports the prayer's request for faith that holds fast beyond what is visible and rests in Christ's priestly work.
This passage calls God's people to trust him rather than lean on their own understanding, which fits the prayer's surrender of self-rule and renewed dependence on the Lord.

sections.heading: Asking you to live through my ordinary life
sections.text: Please make your home in me. Shape what I pray. Fill what I praise. Guard what I say. Direct what I do. Let my life become more and more a place where your presence is seen. Grow me in grace—not only in private thoughts, but in the way I speak, act, choose, and love.
theological_themes: God's presence within the believer transforms prayer, worship, speech, and action.
Growth in grace is practical and whole-life, not merely inward or emotional.
Sanctification depends on abiding in Christ and the work of the Spirit.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that fruitfulness comes from abiding in him, which grounds the prayer's desire for God's life to animate every part of the believer's life.
Paul prays for believers to be strengthened by the Spirit and for Christ to dwell in their hearts through faith, closely matching the request for God to live and work within.
The command to grow in the grace and knowledge of Christ supports the prayer's longing for ongoing spiritual growth rather than stagnation.

sections.heading: Confessing how weak my faith often is
sections.text: You have been generous and kind in helping me believe, but I confess that my faith is often weak. It flickers instead of shining brightly. It stumbles when it should walk steadily. It grows slowly. It turns backward too easily. It should rise toward heaven, but too often it lies in the dust, tangled up in what is small, selfish, and earthly. Lord, breathe on this small spark and make it burn bright.
theological_themes: Even true faith can be weak, unstable, and slow to grow.
The believer honestly confesses spiritual inconsistency and backsliding before God.
God is asked to strengthen the faith he has already given.

scripture_references.connection: The father's cry to Jesus holds together real faith and honest unbelief, making it an apt biblical model for confessing weak, wavering trust.
The apostles' request for increased faith supports the prayer's plea that God would strengthen and enlarge faith rather than leave it as it is.
This passage calls believers to lay aside sin and look to Jesus as the founder and perfecter of faith, connecting weak faith with the need to look again to Christ.

sections.heading: Waking my faith so sin loses its power
sections.text: When my faith falls asleep, my heart does not become harmless. It becomes dirty, crowded with desires that want to break loose. Sin grows there like a poisonous tree bearing deadly fruit. The soil of my heart becomes open ground for whatever is earthly and false to take root. So wake my faith up, Lord. Make it strong and active. Fill my soul with the life of heaven until what is impure is driven out and my heart belongs to you more fully.
theological_themes: Neglected or inactive faith leaves the heart vulnerable to sinful desires.
Sin is not treated lightly but as corrupting, fruitful, and deadly.
Living faith, strengthened by God, is part of how impurity is resisted and holiness grows.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the conflict between the desires of the flesh and the Spirit and calls believers to walk by the Spirit, which supports the prayer's plea for faith to be awakened against impurity.
This verse teaches that putting sin to death happens by the Spirit, grounding the prayer's request that God would drive out impurity rather than leaving the believer to self-effort.
Jesus' description of thorns choking the word helps illuminate the image of earthly growth taking over the heart when faith is not active and watchful.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The phrase 'my entitlement to thee' could sound presumptuous in contemporary English. I rendered it as humble confidence of belonging to God in Christ, preserving assurance while avoiding the idea that God is owed to the believer apart from grace.

The original uses very strong images for the sinful heart when faith is inactive: uncleanness, lusts, poisonous fruit, and tares. I retained the severity because it is central to the prayer's Puritan theology of indwelling sin, though the language was made more natural.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted 'covenant God' as God binding himself to his people through his promises, rather than expanding it into a detailed covenant theology system not explicit in the prayer.

I treated the request for God to 'live and move within me' as a prayer for the indwelling work of Christ by the Spirit in sanctification, because the original connects God's presence with prayer, praise, speech, action, and growth in grace.
I kept the concrete upward anchor image, connecting it to Hebrews 6, but expressed it as trust fastened in God's unseen presence rather than as a mechanical description of faith.
